Team —

Quick sync to align on Acme Analytics (P0 pilot) and a couple of other near-term closes that are shaping our dedicated sizing ask for next quarter. I pulled the attached delta forecast from Sales Ops and highlighted two scenarios we should treat as hypotheses this week:

- Conservative: Acme signs pilot (monthly) + CloudScale PoC - ~60% of the high-case token volume.
- High-case: Acme converts to reserved capacity within 45 days and CloudScale expands pilot - ~135% of the conservative.

Asks:
1) Dylan — can infra map these scenarios to projected GPU-hour demand (NVIDIA A100-equivalent) and point out where the inflection points are (burst vs reserved) by Friday EOD?
2) Marissa / Ben — what are the operational constraints for adding burst slots vs committing reserved capacity for the high-case? Any 2–3 day lead times we should bake into the plan?
3) Laura — rough-dollar run rate delta for the two scenarios (server + cloud egress + license) so Sales can price guardrails.

I attached acme-delta-forecast.xlsx with the scenario sheets. If you prefer a short call, proposing Friday 10 am PT. Otherwise please reply with notes in-thread.

Thanks —

Jordan —

Thanks for the scenario file, I ran a quick mapping assuming an average request size and 1.8x token overhead for chat. High-level notes:

- Conservative: ~38 A100-equivalent GPU-hours/day sustained peak; fits inside existing burst pool but will start to impact other pilots if sustained > 10 days.
- High-case: peaks at ~92 A100-equivalent GPU-hours/day; requires adding at least 8 reserved slots (4-week lead to request hardware allocation) or a dedicated burst reservation with CloudScale (stopgap).

Critical inflection points: sustained 24–48 hour peaks above 50 GPU-hours/day push us from burst-friendly to reserved-friendly — because continuous batching loses efficiency and queue latencies increase. If Acme shows >50% of high-case in first 30 days, we should move to reserved.

I'll drop a short runbook excerpt in the shared Drive (burst vs reserve decision matrix). For now: Friday 2pm PT handoff to Hardware Ops makes sense if we see the high-case probability >30%.

—Dylan

Jordan / team —

Couple of operational points from capacity planning:
- Adding reserved slots: procurement + rack allocation + networking changes together ~= 3–4 weeks if we need physical capacity in our dedicated pool. If it's in-cloud reserved, ~7–10 business days but with capacity approval dependency.
- Burst credits: we can grant up to 200% short-term burst, but that degrades tail latency for other reserved customers; we should attach SLA caveats in the Engagement Plan.

I've attached a short table (pasted below) with lead times and suggested immediate mitigation steps. If Acme signals high-case by Tuesday, Ben and I recommend a two-step approach: 1) secure a burst uplift for the first 2–3 weeks, 2) trigger reserved procurement if usage trajectory stays above the 50-GPU-hour/day threshold.

Marissa Cole
Capacity & Ops Manager, Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com

---
Lead-time summary (excerpt):
- Reserved (on-prem style): 3–4 weeks
- Reserved (cloud reserved instances): 7–10 business days + approval
- Burst uplift (operational): 1–2 business days to approve, effective immediately once provisioned

Quick finance delta for the two scenarios (high-level; will add line items to shared model):

- Conservative: incremental monthly run rate ~$18k (compute + egress + margin).
- High-case (reserved conversion): incremental monthly run rate ~$52k but unit cost drops ~32% once reserved pricing applied; capital timing shifts to committed billing which affects ARR recognition and discount mechanics.

Notes: procurement timelines and minimum commit bands matter — if we commit to a 12-month reserved slab, Sales should protect against churn (in-contract SLAs + early-exit credits). I'll add a sensitivity tab in the Drive + link it to the HubSpot deal record.
